item.title: Assemble covers miniature agricultural buildings in intense blue pigment for Building Blue exhibition in Tokyo
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth exploration of a unique pigment and its application in architecture, with clear and engaging language.

Assemble covers miniature agricultural buildings in intense blue pigment for Building Blue exhibition in Tokyo

Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that “play with scale” to showcase a new pigment made from industrial waste at Tokyo‘s SKAC gallery.

With the exhibition, the UK-based collective said it aimed to “explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour”.

The architects are using the Building Blue exhibition to showcase a new pigment, made by design studio Matter at hand for Assemble from local waste material. It will also be used in Assemble’s Play Earth Park – a campsite under development in rural Japan.

“The pigment was essentially created by analysing local material waste streams in Toyama and exploring what kind of different colours could be produced from them,” Assemble co-founder Maria Lisogorskaya told Dezeen.

“In the end, the blue uses a combination of rice husk ash, limestone filter dust, recycled glass and copper, which are mixed together with water to form a thick clay-like paste and then heated in an electric kiln to around 950ºC,” she continued.

“The materials react to form a new crystal phase – known as cuprorivaite, which is bright blue.”

To show it off, the designers constructed numerous miniature houses from Japanese cedar that draw on the agricultural buildings found close to where the pigment material was sourced.

“The form of the structures plays with the agricultural buildings within the dispersed settlement of rural Toyama; these buildings evolve over time, adapting to what’s needed, often evolving interesting geometries,” Assemble co-founder Lewis Jones told Dezeen.

“We tried to play with scale and make the buildings surreal, creating miniature versions of them for play.”

The buildings have deliberately simple yet evocative geometries that nod to the structures that inspired them. Among them is a barn-like building surrounded by hay bales.

Assemble’s aim was for visitors to be able to climb and explore the structures.

“We hope that the buildings are climbed on and inhabited; and this exhibition is the beginning of the structures’ life as a play space outside SKWAT,” Lisogorskaya said.

“The spirit of resourcefulness, fun, and reimagining of our environments is at the core of the project and we look forward to seeing how the structures are used in ways we didn’t expect.”

The exhibition, which also showcases raw materials used to create the blue colour and products covered in it, is on show in Skwat Kameari Art Centre (SKAC’s) Park gallery in Kameari, Tokyo.

Assemble said it chose to showcase it here as it feels the gallery has a similar spirit to its own UK bases.

“We think SKAC is an amazing interdisciplinary space, and its spirit resonates with how we have set up our studios and labs in London and Liverpool,” Jones said.

“Bringing together design, material experimentation with other arts practices as a more satisfying and richer way of being in the city,” he continued.

SKAC recently opened two new gallery spaces, Material Matters (MM) and Space III, as part of a major extension.

The east Tokyo gallery has previously shown exhibitions including anime-informed chairs by Kwangho Lee and reading spaces by Herzog & de Meuron.

Building Blue is at SKAC, 3-26-4 Kameari, Katsushika-ku, Tokyo 125-0002, from 7 November 2026 to 28 February 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Photography by Daisuke Shima

item.description:

Why it is here: Comprehensive coverage of the Thermory Design Awards with specific examples and design details.

Thermory Design Awards 2026 recognises striking examples of architecture and design using thermowood

A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood.

Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.

Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.

The treatment enhances the material’s dimensional stability and reduces moisture uptake compared with untreated wood, according to Thermory.

The winner of the interior category is a trio of Ukrainian guesthouses collectively named Under the Reed Roof, designed by Kyiv-based studio YOD Group.

Each guesthouse comprises a glass-walled volume at the base, topped by a tapered thatched roof with exaggerated proportions.

While the exterior of these roofs is made with traditional reeds, the interiors are lined with thermo-ash shingles, arranged to create a tactile effect that is repeated on the front doors.

These highlight the interplay between the interior’s traditional and contemporary design elements, contrasting materials, and the balance between the structure’s openness and enclosure.

“The project stood out to the jury for its exceptionally coherent concept, in which architecture and interior elements come together to form a harmonious whole,” said Thermory.

Winning in the tiny and private house category was Marker Architecture‘s Flooded Gums project, a flood-resilient dwelling built on working farmland.

The building features thermo-ash cladding and thermo-spruce decking, owing to the materials’ robustness and aesthetic merits.

“What particularly impressed the jury was the honesty and clarity of the architecture,” said Thermory of the project.

“Rather than concealing its construction, the project makes its structural logic visible, with every element serving a purpose: the result is a modest yet highly refined building that strikes a compelling balance between aesthetics, functionality and its natural setting,” it added.

Estonia’s Rakke Kindergarten secured the win in the residential, commercial and public building category, thanks to what Thermory describes as local studio Arhitekt Must‘s “cohesive and imaginative design”.

Thermo-spruce cladding, thermo-pine posts and thermo-pine decking all feature in the design, enhancing both its functionality and visual appeal.

The building’s function as an educational environment is made distinctive by the space’s inventive ceiling, which is composed of the short thermo-pine posts, arranged in a way that creates an engaging optical illusion.

“This unexpected architectural gesture elevates a functional space into something distinctive, demonstrating how thoughtful detailing can shape the character and experience of an entire building,” said Thermory.

Finally, the winner of the wellness and spa category is a sauna within the Estonian Embassy in Berlin, designed by interior studio AERIS.

The interiors feature statement walls covered in custom-made oak shingles, which, being circular and slightly overlapping, resemble fish scales.

These are joined by thermo-alder benches and walls, creating a cohesive scheme of timber details that integrate neatly with the lighting design.

“The harmonious interplay of materials, surfaces and light imbues the space with a contemporary edge while retaining the intimacy and warmth of a traditional sauna,” said Thermory.

“Although vastly different in character and purpose, the winning projects share a creative and unconventional approach to design,” it added.

“Each places wood at the heart of its architectural expression, combining imaginative thinking with meticulous attention to detail.”

The 2026 instalment of the competition was judged by a diverse international jury of architects and Thermory representatives, including Kärt Kanarbik, Thermory’s architectural project manager; Lars Skjølstrup Østergaard, lead design architect at Henning Larsen; Sami Rintala, professor and architect at Rintala Eggertsson Architects; Jaan Port, architect and partner at PIN Arhitektid; and Tõnis Kalve, architect at ByKalve and Thermory project sales architect.

To learn more about Thermory, visit its website.

item.title: The Volvo EX60 Draws on Forest Walks and Nordic Seas
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging narrative about the Volvo EX60's design inspiration, with a focus on natural elements and Scandinavian design principles.

“Scandinavian design never shouts, but when you come closer, you are rewarded,” says Sara Erichsen Susnjar, senior color and material design manager at Volvo Cars. Detail by detail, the automaker’s new all-electric EX60 bears this out. Its seats carry a pattern drawn from two seas converging off the coast of Skagen, Denmark; its base carpet borrows its hue from foraged finds from the woods outside the company’s studio in Sweden; and an interior lighting option fills the cabin with the silhouettes of leaves.

Erichsen Susnjar, who has spent 20 years at Volvo Cars, oversaw color and materials for both the EX60 and the EX60 Cross Country. Under her direction, the team looked to the natural world for the car’s colors, patterns, and textures, often starting with what turned up on a walk.

Forest Finds

Gathering began close to home, on outings that were already part of the team’s routine. “We are very fortunate to have the forest just outside our design studio, so it naturally becomes part of our everyday life, whether we go there for lunch, a coffee break, or simply to clear our minds,” Erichsen Susnjar says.

Over time, the team began bringing small pieces of the landscape back inside: mushrooms, twigs, stones, moss, and herbs. Each was studied for its pattern, color, and texture, then cast or digitized, and the findings became prompts for new ideas. Traces of the work appear in subtle patterns on the seatbacks and door panels, as well as in the shade of the base carpet. As Erichsen Susnjar puts it, “In that sense, a little piece of the forest has found its way into the car.”

Material Choices

Inside the cabin, material options include tailored wool-blend upholstery and ash wood decor, which sit alongside a 15-inch curved OLED display with Google built-in. “I think bringing natural materials into such a technical and precise environment creates a beautiful contrast,” Erichsen Susnjar explains. “They bring warmth, character and, in a way, a soul to the car. Because natural materials have their own variations and imperfections, they can never be exactly replicated, which means every interior becomes slightly unique.”

Erichsen Susnjar places the cabin’s finer details, including its piping, within a longer regional tradition. “Scandinavian design is very much about those subtle touches,” she says. “They don’t demand your attention, but you discover them over time.”

The EX60 offers six lighting colors, along with Forest Leaves Projection, which brings a canopy of foliage into the interior. The idea came from one of the specialist designers at Volvo Cars, and the team expanded on it to explore how the cabin might feel immersed in woodland.

Outside the cabin, the EX60’s exterior paint colors, among them Forest Lake and Heather Bronze, were developed as a palette that balances light and dark, warm and cool, and complements the colors chosen for the interior. Heather Bronze takes its cue from metals weathered over time and the warm cast of heather fields in autumn.

Crossing Waves

The EX60’s signature motif began when members of the team visited Skagen, where the Skagerrak and Kattegat seas meet, and observed the patterns created by their intersecting waves. Early sketches were refined into a pattern that now appears across the car. It is perforated into the ventilated Nordico upholstery and applied to the subwoofer mesh, the decor panels of the Core version, the rubber floor mats, and the knitted, ventilated seats of the EX60 Cross Country.

Beyond its connection to the Danish coastline, the crossing-wave form also proved useful in production. “There is another layer in this story, and that’s how a pattern like crossing waves was perfect for optimizing the cutting of the materials and minimizing waste,” Erichsen Susnjar says. “And because of that, none of the seats look the same.”

item.description:

Why it is here: Listicle with a focus on gift ideas, which does not meet the criteria for original reporting or in-depth analysis.

The Best Gifts for Cooks, Chefs, and the Culinary Curious

Design Milk’s Taste columnist TJ Girard brings her perspective on food and design to this year’s gift guide, selecting thoughtful finds for home cooks, professional chefs, and anyone who loves gathering around the table.

The holiday season brings plenty of opportunities to gather around the table, and for those who love to cook, eat, and experiment in the kitchen, there’s no shortage of gift possibilities. A good gift should feel personal, whether it’s an object they’ll use for years or an ingredient worth sharing around the table.

This year’s selections come with stories of their own. There’s a Oaxacan potter who grows copal and tobacco to finish his clay, a Norwegian fisherman’s daughter who became convinced seaweed is the food of the future, and a former line cook who declared she had an apron company before she actually did.

You’ll find serving pieces that make entertaining easier, ingredients that start conversations, and small but indispensable kitchen tools that prove thoughtful doesn’t have to mean extravagant. Some are made for the table, others for the kitchen, and a few might inspire an entirely new culinary adventure.

After all, the best gifts give everyone something to enjoy, whether it’s a new flavor to try or a good story to share.

Oaxacan Clay Mezcal Set by Francisco for Obakki // Agave Worm Salt by SOS Chefs // El Mero Mero Espadín

Mezcal deserves a proper vessel, and Francisco’s hand-built clay set brings generations of Oaxacan pottery traditions to the table. After learning the craft from his family and spending years away, the artisan returned home to work with the same earth his ancestors used. He uses his community’s traditional kilns and adds something of his own: copal and tobacco he grows by hand. Their sap and leaves create the smoky black finish, while shades of cream, orange, and aqua come from natural elements sourced at a nearby mine. That’s the magic of Oaxaca. Every potter has a particular source of mud and sand, so no two studios look alike.

The set for Obakki includes a carafe, platter, four cups, and a small bowl for gusano salt. To complete the gift, add a bottle of El Mero Mero Espadín, a 48% ABV Oaxacan mezcal with cooked-maguey smoke, herbal notes, and a very long finish that the producer pairs with moles, adobos, and spicy seafood. Then add Agave Worm Salt from SOS Chefs for rimming, dipping, or sprinkling over orange slices. Sip, nibble, repeat.

The Oaxacan Clay Mezcal Set is available at obakki.com for $193; the El Mero Mero Espadín is available at drinkfellows.com for $65; and the Agave Worm Salt is available from sos-chefs.com for $20.

Tecali Mortar and Pestle by Obakki

Have a friend obsessed with guacamole? Someone who makes pesto the long way, with a lot of garlic and a little attitude? Carved from solid Mexican lava rock and paired with a Tzalam wood pestle, the Tecali Mortar and Pestle is exactly what they need. Weighing in at nine pounds, with the rough, textured surface of a traditional molcajete, it’s a kitchen tool built to last.

The piece comes from a Mexico City design collective that works with woodworkers from Veracruz and Mérida and stone carvers from Puebla. Designer Karim Molina begins every piece by exploring the raw material itself. Guacamole made in this bowl tastes better—or at least feels like it does, which amounts to the same thing at a party.

The Tecali Mortar and Pestle is available at obakki.com for $210.

Orbelle Etagere by Ferm Living

A tiered stand screams special occasion. Ferm Living’s Orbelle Etagere pairs mirror-polished stainless steel with a tiered design, so everything you stack on it catches the candlelight. Give grandma’s cream puffs the moment they’ve always deserved, or create a tower of glassware beside your self-serve bar setup. At 14.2 inches tall and approximately 11.8 inches wide, it’s substantial enough to serve as a centerpiece but arrives flat-packed for easy storage.

The Orbelle Etagere is available at fermliving.us for $209.

Cookware Collection by Hedley & Bennett

Every great brand has an origin story, and Hedley & Bennett’s begins with a bluff. When her head chef announced he was ordering new aprons, Ellen Marie Bennett, then a 24-year-old line cook, told him she had an apron company. She didn’t, at least not yet. What she did have was the willingness to leap and then figure it out on the way down. More than a decade later, the brand has expanded beyond its signature kitchen uniforms with its first cookware collection.

The lineup combines five-ply stainless steel cookware with enameled cast iron, balancing responsive heating with serious heat retention. Available in Shiso Green, Enoki White, and French Blue, the pieces bring the brand’s signature use of color to the stovetop. They’re oven-safe to 550°F and designed for everything from weeknight meals to ambitious dinner parties. The collection is built for people who are figuring it out as they go, which, if you ask Ellen, is how everything great gets started.

The Full Cookware 6-Piece Set is available at hedleyandbennett.com for $530, with individual pieces starting at $150.

Ice Cream Cup 02 and Canteen Table Spoons by Service Projects

Stainless steel serveware is as functional as it is stunning. Composed of two complementary forms that give it both stability and sculptural presence, the ice cream cup from Service Projects is equally suited to a scoop of French vanilla or a small mound of buttery Castelvetrano olives.

Pair four cups with the brand’s Canteen Polished Table Spoons for a touch of Art Deco elegance at the table. It’s the perfect gift for the friend who loves making homemade ice cream or is taking their chocolate mousse recipe to the grave.

The Ice Cream Cup 02 ($35 each; $140 for a set of four) and the Canteen Polished Table Spoon ($75 for a set of four) are available at na.service-projects.com.…
